dimensions.note: applicationKey is .meta({ sensitive: true }) and documented as vault-sourced; it is never echoed into a payload, a snapshot or a log line. The 24h authorizationToken is treated as the bearer credential it is: sent only in the Authorization header, never persisted. Asserted by execution, not by reading — 'no method leaks a secret into a snapshot or a log line' drives all six methods and greps every write and log for both secrets, and 'the bearer token is sent as a header and never as a body field' checks every non-authorize request. The mechanical harness repeats the credential grep independently. B2 never returns SSE-C key material, so no file payload can carry one. Residual, documented rather than fixed: fileInfo is arbitrary user metadata that B2 stores with each file and returns on every read, so it lands in a snapshot verbatim — the README warns it must never hold a credential, matching the bucketInfo precedent in @sntxrr/b2/bucket.

Structured throughout: message templates with named placeholders and a props object, never string concatenation of values. Warnings are reserved for facts an operator must not miss and each names the consequence rather than the symptom — truncation says the counts are a FLOOR, hide says the data underneath is still stored and billed, non-current bytes name the lifecycle rule that would reap them, and a requested-but-invisible bucket is warned rather than skipped silently. One defect found and fixed during this review: update accepted bypassGovernance alongside a legal-hold-only change and dropped it silently, which would leave an operator believing a governance lock had been overridden when nothing was attempted; it now warns, covered by a test.

b2Fetch throws Error & { status, b2Code } and the model branches on the code, never on message text. 401 unauthorized is deliberately not retried — a missing capability is not transient, and the README maps each method to the capabilities it needs so the fix is the key's grant. Guards throw sentences that state what was refused and how to proceed, not assertion failures. Ordering was audited: every gate (destruction, compliance, detailed-mode prefix/maxFiles, REPLACE-without-contentType) fires before any B2 call, asserted by tests that check calls.length === 0. One real ordering defect was found and fixed: copy resolved the destination bucket's NAME after the copy had already landed, so a lookup failure would have stranded a completed side effect behind a failed method; the resolution now happens first, with a test asserting b2_copy_file was never issued.

86 tests, all mocked — no live B2. CONVENTIONS §10 items 1-7 are all covered (nested v4 auth shape, null allowed.buckets, flat v2/v3 body rejected, two-page drain with next*->start* renaming across BOTH cursor halves, page-cap truncation, exactly-one re-auth on expired_auth_token, 429 with Retry-After, non-transient 400 carrying b2Code, idempotent delete, no secret leaks). The harness validates every write against the real spec schema per §10.1, and was proven to bite by mutation rather than assumed: stringifying a derived byte count failed 12 tests with the schema-rejection message, and a schema-LEGAL semantic regression (reporting 0 instead of null for unmeasured non-current data — the wave-1 unprunedPrefixes bug class) failed exactly the two tests written to catch it. Both mutations were reverted and the suite re-verified green.

scan and sync are read-only and naturally repeatable. delete is idempotent per CONVENTIONS §3: a 404, or a 400 with b2Code file_not_present or no_such_file, is a success that still writes the exists=false tombstone, and a name that resolves to nothing skips the call entirely. isAlreadyGone deliberately excludes bad_bucket_id — that is a configuration bug, and swallowing it would report a successful delete of a file still sitting in the bucket the caller meant; asserted directly. reauth is threaded through every call site so a long fleet drain survives the 24h token expiring mid-scan. hide and copy are not idempotent by nature (each writes a new version) and are documented as such rather than pretending otherwise.

Built against the v4 corrections in CONVENTIONS §4 rather than Backblaze's own prose. The canonical client (§5) was verified byte-identical to b2-account, b2-bucket and b2-key by diff after formatting, so no local drift was introduced. The authorization-wrapper trap (§4.3) is handled generically by unwrapAuthorized for fileRetention and legalHold, which distinguishes absent (null) from unreadable (false) from readable, and the aggregate counts unreadable locks separately — an unreadable hold is never counted as off. The slim-response trap is handled: b2_update_file_legal_hold and b2_update_file_retention return only the id, name and changed field, so update re-reads via the class-B b2_get_file_info rather than snapshotting a hollowed-out body; asserted. defaultRetention/fileRetention is modelled as an object, not a string (§4.6). Unverified against live B2: this model has not yet been run against a real account, so per PRD §7 item 3 its derived fields carry exactly the risk that found six defects in wave 1. Flagged as the next step, not as a passed gate.

Two specs, cleanly separated by what they describe: aggregate is per-bucket/per-prefix inventory, file is one immutable file VERSION. scan is a genuine factory — one execution fans out across every bucket the key can see and acquires the per-model lock once, rather than N contending runs (CLAUDE.md rule 6). Cost is designed against and reported, not hidden: class-C transactions are counted honestly (one per 1000 files, so a 10000-file page bills as ten), the default page size is the B2 maximum because it costs the same as ten small pages while making a tenth of the round trips, and detailed mode stops listing once maxFiles is in hand so it does not pay to enumerate a million versions and discard all but a thousand. Aggregate mode is the default precisely because per-file emission over a restic repo would write tens of thousands of snapshots.

Every fixture and README example uses example.com-class names and fake-but-plausible B2 identifiers (example-backup-bucket, 4a48fe8875c6214145260818, a1b2c3d4e5f6, K004example...). No real bucket name, account ID, key ID or homelab hostname appears in the model, the tests, the README or the mechanical harness. Grepped the published archive contents; the only real-world specifics are the restic path conventions (data/, index/, snapshots/), which are public properties of restic's on-disk format, not of this account.

Deliberately calibrated per CONVENTIONS §4.9 — permissive where the shape is unobserved, strict where it is documented and observed. Byte and count fields are z.number().int() because B2 documents contentLength as an integer and a non-integer there would be a genuine contract change worth failing on; that trade-off is adjudicated, not accidental. The honest-null contract is enforced in the schema itself: every version-derived metric is .nullable() and the descriptions say null means 'not measured', never zero. serverSideEncryption and fileInfo are held loosely (only mode is projected; a non-object fileInfo degrades to {}) so an unexpected shape cannot sink a 24-bucket scan. Field coverage is verified by execution: the mechanical harness diffs each spec's schema keys against the keys actually written and confirms 1:1 in both directions, plus per-write completeness and a live safeParse of every write.

Both specs are lifetime 'infinite' with garbageCollection 50, matching b2-bucket and b2-key. That is right for aggregate, whose value is the trend — 50 versions of a per-bucket byte total is the series that shows whether the hidden-version debt is growing or being reaped. For file it is effectively moot in detailed mode: a fileId is immutable and never revisited, so each instance accumulates exactly one version and the cap never binds. The consequence is instance-count growth rather than version growth, which is inherent to per-file emission and is why detailed mode is opt-in and hard-capped by a required maxFiles.

Covers all eight operations PRD §4 assigns to this model: b2_list_file_names and b2_list_file_versions (scan), b2_get_file_info (sync/update re-read), b2_delete_file_version (delete), b2_hide_file (hide), b2_copy_file (copy), b2_update_file_legal_hold and b2_update_file_retention (update). Method names follow the PRD rather than the §3 taxonomy for hide and copy, which is a deliberate, documented divergence — see preflight-checks. Deliberately out of scope and stated as such: b2_copy_file is capped by B2 at 5 GB, and the large-file copy path belongs to @sntxrr/b2/transfer in wave 3.

Three checks, all labelled policy: credentials-present, file-destruction-acknowledged (appliesTo delete) and single-bucket-for-file-methods (appliesTo delete, update). Their limits are documented rather than papered over, because both limits are real. First, swamp never gives a check the method's inputs, so a check cannot see --input allowFileDestruction=true and cannot be what enforces; the actual gates live in execute (assertDestructionAllowed, assertComplianceAllowed) and the checks exist only to fail fast when the MODEL is misconfigured. Second, pre-flight checks fire only for methods named create/update/delete/action, so no check can ever guard hide — its gate is unconditionally inside execute, and the method description says so. Tests cover both the globalArgs path and the method-input path for each gate, and assert that both fire before any B2 call.

Every instance is spec-prefixed per CONVENTIONS §2, since instance names share one flat storage namespace across specs and one scan writes both. aggregate names additionally carry an FNV-1a hash of the raw (bucketName, group) pair, because a prefix group is user-controlled text containing slashes that must be sanitized to be path-safe and sanitization is lossy — 'data/' and 'data_' reduce alike and are kept distinct by the hash, asserted by test. The bucket-wide total is encoded with a sentinel that no B2 prefix can produce, making a total-versus-root-group collision structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely. file keys on fileId, never fileName, because a name has arbitrarily many versions and keying by name would make a detailed scan's versions overwrite each other. The reserved literal 'latest' is unreachable (every name is prefixed), asserted directly and re-checked by the mechanical harness, which also proves no single execution writes the same instance twice — the failure that made b2-bucket's notification snapshot eat its bucket snapshot.

Resources are shaped for CEL querying: scalar, introspectable fields rather than nested blobs, so the questions this model exists to answer are one predicate each. The README gives the two that matter — filtering on nonCurrentBytes != null && > 0 to find buckets paying for data they no longer serve, and on truncated == true to check whether that number is even complete. The nullable-metric contract is what makes those queries safe: a null cannot be mistaken for a zero by a > 0 filter, which is precisely how the wave-1 unprunedPrefixes bug hid all 24 buckets from exactly this kind of query. Authorization flags sit beside their values so a consumer can distinguish 'unlocked' from 'not allowed to look'.

First publish at 2026.08.05.1 — no prior version exists in the registry, so there is no compatibility surface to break and the version-drift check is expected to report none. Forward-looking commitments recorded here so a later change is visibly breaking rather than quietly so: the nullable non-current metrics are a contract (a future version must not start reporting 0 for unmeasured data), file instances are keyed by fileId (re-keying would orphan every existing snapshot), and adding an aggregate field is additive while narrowing a nullable one is not. The four nested-blob element shapes remain unmodelled pending live observation, consistent with CONVENTIONS §4.9, so typing them later is an additive change.
